label: in0-early-probe
_why: THE EARLY-GAME in0 PROBE (user-proposed 2026-09-19: 'running a 1836-1838 probe to understand where the very early game stabilises (do we hit our prediction for dead industries, what are realised margins, is world product significantly distorted) is not [2.5 hours]. In fact, we could run a dozen 2+1 probes of this type to understand the early-game effects of different in0.'). F140 bounded the era-0 input penalty ON PAPER - at vanilla's measured 1836/1840 prices the insolvent share of the 70 (industry x market) cells goes 31% (vanilla's own recipe) -> 41% (in0 1.2, the canon) -> 54% (1.4) -> 56% (1.6), the seven markets' era-0 VALUE ADDED goes 100 -> 79 -> 58 -> 37% of vanilla's, and nothing is 'very dead' on the scalar axis up to x1.5. EVERY ONE OF THOSE IS A PREDICTION MADE AT FIXED PRICES WHILE THE RECIPE MOVED, which is exactly the thing BALANCE_FRAMEWORK 10.86.2 says not to trust: the penalty raises its own input prices (first-order, British fabric 92 -> 122% of base at x1.4) and shrinks its own buildings, and neither feedback is in the census. Two in-game years is enough to see both. This batch measures what the paper says, at four penalties, against a vanilla control taken at the SAME dump dates.

_arms.vanilla: {kind: control} - vanilla + telemetry and nothing else. Included even though the n=16 baseline exists, because THAT baseline's market dumps are 1836.2.1 and then 1840.1.1 with nothing between, and the whole question here is the path in between. Its save summaries (yearly) do give world GDP at 1837 and 1838, so the world-product comparison has a second, independent source.
_arms.probe-in12: {kind: config, config: config/mod_config.canon-c19-in12.json} - THE SHIPPED CANON, in0 1.2. The reference arm: every other arm differs from it in one field.
_arms.probe-in14: {kind: config, config: config/mod_config.probe-in14.json} - in0 1.4 (F140's recommended point)

_delta: ONE FIELD. Generated by make_ab_config with the canon's own command and --in0 changed; verified field-by-field against the canon: `inputs` and `target_be` on all 56 rungs, nothing else - not cost, not ai_value, not a define, not a technology. A 2.2 / B 1.5 / cost anchor x 1.9^era / ai_value 1000x3^era / divisor 0.000125 / the 10.75 defines / the 24-month bar are the canon's throughout.

_predictions._basis: All from FINDINGS F140 (the era-0 solvency census) unless stated. They are stated BEFORE the runs so a surprise is a finding and not a correction.
_predictions.world_product: 1838 world GDP vs the vanilla arm: in12 0.97-1.03x. The census's first-order VA arithmetic (the seven markets' era-0 value added is 9.2% of world GDP, and the penalty subtracts it one-for-one) predicts each +0.1 of in0 costs ~0.7-0.9 points, so in13 0.96-1.02, in14 0.94-1.00, in15 0.92-0.99. FAILURE MODE and the thing worth learning: a cost materially LARGER than that means the feedbacks (dearer inputs, shed workers, less construction) amplify rather than damp, and the whole in0 axis is more expensive than the paper says.
_predictions.dead_industries: The share of TIERED building types running a negative margin at 1838 (from each save summary's per-type profit and va_out, F92's identity). Predicted from the census at vanilla's settled 1840 prices: in12 ~20-30%, in13 ~30-40%, in14 ~40-50%, in15 ~45-60%. NAMED PREDICTIONS: glass is negative in the vanilla arm too (its 1836 median is -21% on vanilla's own recipe); steel and artillery are the next to go; food and textile stay positive in every arm.
_predictions.very_dead: NO tiered building type at a margin below -20% that is still negative after its output price could triple, in any arm including in15 - the census finds none on the scalar axis up to x1.5 at vanilla prices, and only 1 (Dutch steel, which is negative in vanilla too) at the mod's own. A very-dead type appearing in in13 or in14 would falsify the census's central claim.
_predictions.realised_margins: Realised era-0 margin at 1838, world, by the F92 identity. The DESIGNED base-price margins are median +5% (in12), -3% (in13), -10% (in14), -16% (in15); realised will be far ABOVE them because early prices sit above base (groceries 175% of base in the British market at 1836, iron 147%). Predict e0 realised 25-40% at in12, falling 4-8 points per +0.1 of in0. ⭐ THE READING THAT MATTERS is the SLOPE, not the level: if realised margins move ~1:1 with the designed cut then in0 is a usable dial; if the market absorbs most of it (F139's compression, where a designed 5/55/127/233 realised as 26/31/47/46) then in0 is a weak dial on margins and its cost to the anchor is being paid for little.
_predictions.input_prices: British fabric and wood, % of base, at 1838. First-order the census puts fabric 92 -> 108 (in12) -> 122 (in14) -> 137 (in16); predict the realised move is SMALLER because the raw sector answers within two years. Wood and fabric rising faster than that is the amplifying case.
_predictions.staffing: Tiered staffed levels and workers at 1838 fall monotonically with in0; the loss-makers shed employment rather than disappearing (the engine lays off before it demolishes), so watch STAFFING not level counts.

_reads: Per run: save summaries every quarter (8 per run) give world GDP, per-building-type profit / va_out / va_in / staffing / levels; market dumps at five dates give prices, buy/sell and production per good in the seven markets. `node tools/era0_solvency.mjs --van <this session> --date 1838.1.1` re-runs the census against the arm's OWN realised prices, which is the direct paper-vs-game comparison.
_comparison: The vanilla arm of this batch at the same dates (primary); the n=16 vanilla baseline 20260821_131149 for world GDP at 1837/1838 and for prices at 1836.2.1 (independent second source); FINDINGS F140 for every prediction above.
_watch: run 1 at ~3 min: mod marker in debug.log, game version, this run's error window BY POSITION, clock advancing
after the first mod run: era0_solvency against its own prices, and the per-type margins at 1838
post-batch: preflight -Session, VERDICT.md, SESSION_VERDICTS row, FINDINGS
_cost: 14 runs x 1836->1838 (2 in-game years, ~1 in-game year per minute at the opening rate) ~ 4-6 min each including build, launch and harvest ~ 75-90 min total.
_caveats: TWO IN-GAME YEARS IS NOT THE CENTURY. It answers where the early game lands, not whether a book works: obsolescence, the price decline and the hoard are all century-scale and NOTHING here speaks to them.

The 1836 supply anchor is broken in every A-ladder book (F137), so all four mod arms carry the same +27.3% over-production; the probe compares them to each other and to vanilla with that defect present in all of them.
Seed spread at this horizon is small (F140: 10 pp of base price across 16 vanilla seeds at 1836.2.1, against 61 pp across markets), so n=3 per mod arm is generous and n=2 for the control is enough.

Launch ONLY through tools/testbed/launch_detached.ps1 CALLED DIRECTLY from the PowerShell tool (landmine L30); the STOP file must be absent. No run-level stop applies - a two-year run cannot run away.

defaults._dump_dates_note: 1836.2.1 is the anchor instant the whole vanilla baseline shares; the rest trace the stabilisation. The last is 1837.12.1 rather than 1838.1.1 so it cannot race the run's own end date.
